chapters.title: Chapter 3: Corporate Tax Rates and Regimes

lessons.title: The Concessional 22% Regime vs the Old Regime With Deductions

body.text: The 22% regime is not a discount. It is a trade. You hand back almost every incentive the tax law offers, and in exchange you get a lower rate and a simpler life. Whether that trade is worth taking depends on one number: how much you were actually claiming.

children.text: When the government cut the corporate rate in September 2019, it did not simply lower everyone's tax. It offered a second regime alongside the old one. Take 22% under section 200 [old 115BAA] and surrender your deductions, or stay at 25% or 30% and keep them. Most companies moved. Some were right not to.

body.caption: Incentives surrendered when a company opts into section 200 [old 115BAA]
headers: Who it used to matter to

cells: Additional depreciation of 20% on new plant and machinery
Deduction for units in special economic zones
IT services and export businesses with SEZ units
Companies that set up in notified backward areas or specified sectors
Pharma, chemicals and engineering R&D units
Most profit-linked deductions of the deductions chapter
Brought forward losses and depreciation attributable to those incentives
Any company carrying such losses from earlier years

body.text: Accumulated minimum alternate tax credit used to belong on this list, because it was forfeited on entering the 22% regime. The Finance Act, 2026 turned that around. From tax year 2026-27, old MAT credit can be used only by a company that has moved into the concessional regime, capped at 25% of that year's tax liability, while a company staying in the old regime cannot use it at all. Any advice written before 2026 says the opposite, so check the date on anything you read about this.

children.text: The surrender is narrower than most founders assume. Ordinary business expenditure is untouched, because those are costs of earning income, not incentives. Two specific deductions also survive, and both matter.

columns.label: Ordinary deductions, untouched
points: Salaries, rent, power, freight and every running cost under section 34 [old 37(1)]
Interest on business borrowings under section 32 [old 36]
Normal depreciation at the usual rates under section 33 [old 32]
Statutory dues and bonus, on actual payment under section 37 [old 43B]

columns.label: Incentives that survive the switch
points: Section 146 [old 80JJAA], the deduction for additional employee cost when you add staff
Section 148 [old 80M], the deduction for dividends received from other domestic companies and passed on
No minimum alternate tax under section 206 [old 115JB] applies at all
Accumulated MAT credit, usable here but nowhere else, capped at 25% of the year's tax liability
A flat 10% surcharge, so no jump at ₹10 crore of income

body.text: Section 146 [old 80JJAA] deserves attention from HR as much as finance. A company adding employees can claim an extra 30% of the additional employee cost as a deduction, for three consecutive years, on top of the salaries already claimed. It survives inside the 22% regime, and it is routinely missed because the finance team never sees the hiring data in the right format.

children.text: The decision reduces to a single comparison. In the old regime you pay a higher rate on a smaller number. In the new one you pay a lower rate on the whole thing. The question is how big your deductions must be before the higher rate on a smaller base still wins.

body.caption: D is the total incentive deduction, I is taxable income before it. Above this ratio, the old regime wins.
How much deduction you need to justify staying in the old regime
headers: Break-even deduction, as a share of income

body.label: The rule of thumb for a large company
body.context: A company at the 30% base rate with income above ₹10 crore needs incentive deductions worth more than roughly 28% of its taxable income before the old regime beats 25.168%. Very few businesses clear that bar without an SEZ unit or a major expansion.

body.title: Show me the math: ₹10 crore of income, two levels of deduction

children.text: A company earns ₹10,00,00,000 before incentive deductions. In the old regime it pays 30% base with 7% surcharge and 4% cess, an effective 33.384%. In the concessional regime it pays 25.168% on the full amount, with no deductions.

cells: The old regime is cheaper by ₹17,99,200

children.text: The switchover sits at 24.6% of income, which is ₹2,46,00,000 here. Below that, take the lower rate. Above it, keep the deductions. And remember this comparison has to hold for years to come, not just this one, because the choice cannot be undone.

body.title: Try It: Find the Break-Even
body.prompt: A company pays the 25% base rate with income above ₹10 crore, an effective 29.12%. Above what percentage of taxable income must its incentive deductions be for the old regime to beat the 25.168% concessional regime? Answer as a percentage.
body.explanation: Divide 25.168 by 29.120, which gives 0.8643, and subtract from 1 to get 0.1357, or about 13.6%. Notice how much lower this bar is than the 28% a 30% base rate company faces. The smaller your old-regime rate advantage, the less deduction it takes to justify staying put.

body.title: Quick Check: What Survives the Switch?
body.question: A company has just opted into section 200 [old 115BAA]. Which of these can it still claim?
options: Additional depreciation of 20% on the new machines it installed this year
The deduction for additional employee cost under section 146 [old 80JJAA]
The deduction for its special economic zone unit
The weighted deduction for its in-house scientific research
body.explanation: Section 146 [old 80JJAA] survives, which is why growing companies that hire should still track additional employee cost carefully. Additional depreciation, the SEZ deduction and research incentives are all surrendered on entering the regime. Accumulated MAT credit is a separate story: since the Finance Act, 2026 it can be used only inside this regime, and only up to 25% of the year's tax liability.

children.text: The Mechanics, and Why Timing Matters

cells: By filing the prescribed form on or before the due date for the return under section 263(1) [old 139(1)], for the first year you want it to apply
No. The option is irrevocable, for that year and every year after
Must it be filed again each year?
No. Once validly exercised it continues, unless a condition is breached
Yes. A company can stay in the old regime for now and opt in for a future year
No. Section 206 [old 115JB] does not apply to a company taxed under section 200
A company whose option under section 201 [old 115BAB] becomes invalid can fall back to section 200

body.text: Because the option can be exercised in any later year but never withdrawn, the sensible pattern for a company with genuine incentives is to wait. Use the SEZ benefit or the accumulated MAT credit while it is worth something, then opt in once the incentive is exhausted. The gate only opens inwards, so there is no cost to being late and no way back from being early.

body.title: Scenario: The SEZ Unit and the MAT Credit
body.scenario: A Hyderabad IT services company earns ₹14 crore of taxable income a year before deductions. Its SEZ unit still gives it a deduction of about ₹3.5 crore a year, but that benefit runs out in two more years. It also carries ₹90 lakh of accumulated minimum alternate tax credit. Its CFO has been told the company is paying above-market tax and should move to 22% immediately.
body.prompt: Should it switch now, in two years, or not at all?
body.modelAnswer: Switch now, and the MAT credit is the reason. Start with the rate comparison: in the old regime the company pays 34.944% on ₹10.5 crore after the SEZ deduction, about ₹3,66,91,200, while section 200 would cost 25.168% on the full ₹14 crore, about ₹3,52,35,200. So even with the SEZ deduction still running, switching saves roughly ₹14,56,000 a year. That fits the break-even table, since the deduction is 25% of income and this company would need about 28% to justify staying. Then add what changed in 2026. Accumulated MAT credit can now be used only by a company inside the concessional regime, capped at 25% of that year's tax liability, and is simply unusable by a company that stays in the old regime. Here, 25% of ₹3,52,35,200 is ₹88,08,800, so almost the entire ₹90 lakh could be absorbed in the first year and the rest in the second. Staying put to protect the SEZ deduction would leave that ₹90 lakh idle and, once the deduction expires in two years, the old regime would cost about ₹4.89 crore on ₹14 crore against ₹3.52 crore under section 200. Every line points the same way. The company should still model five years before filing, because the option is irrevocable, but the CFO's instinct is right on both the destination and the timing.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The One-Way Door
body.textWithBlank: Once a company exercises the option under section 200 [old 115BAA], that option is ___, so it cannot return to the old regime in a later year.
body.explanation: Irrevocable. That single word is why this decision deserves a multi-year model rather than a comparison of this year's numbers. The only movement the law allows is inwards: a company can join later, and a company whose section 201 option fails can fall back to section 200.

body.title: Before You File the Option
steps: List every incentive deduction actually claimed in the last three years, in rupees, not in principle
Check whether any of them expires soon, such as an SEZ benefit or a three-year employment deduction
Find out how much minimum alternate tax credit is sitting unused, since it can now be used only inside the concessional regime, capped at 25% of the year's tax liability
Identify brought forward losses and depreciation that relate to surrendered incentives, because those go too
Project income and deductions for the next five years, not just this one
Confirm that section 146 [old 80JJAA] and section 148 [old 80M] benefits are being claimed either way
File the prescribed form on or before the return due date under section 263(1) [old 139(1)] for the first year you want the regime to apply

cards.definition: The optional 22% regime for domestic companies, effective 25.168%, in exchange for surrendering most incentives.
A deduction of 30% of additional employee cost for three consecutive years, which survives inside the concessional regime.
A deduction for inter-corporate dividends received and passed on, preventing the same dividend being taxed twice in a group.
Tax paid earlier under minimum alternate tax. From tax year 2026-27 it can be set off only by a company inside the concessional regime, and only up to 25% of that year's tax liability.
The level of incentive deductions, as a share of income, at which the old regime and the 22% regime cost the same.
An election that cannot be withdrawn once made, binding the company for that year and all later years.

points: Section 200 [old 115BAA] trades most incentives for a 22% base rate, an effective 25.168% with flat 10% surcharge and 4% cess
Surrendered items include additional depreciation, SEZ and area-based deductions, research incentives, and brought forward losses related to them
Accumulated MAT credit is no longer forfeited on switching, and since the Finance Act, 2026 it can only be used inside this regime, capped at 25% of the year's tax liability
Ordinary business deductions are untouched, and section 146 [old 80JJAA] and section 148 [old 80M] survive the switch
A company at the 30% base rate needs incentive deductions above roughly 28% of income before the old regime wins, and one at 25% needs only about 13.6%
Minimum alternate tax under section 206 [old 115JB] does not apply inside the concessional regime
The option can be exercised in any future year but never withdrawn, so a company with live incentives should use them first and switch afterwards

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. The list of surrendered incentives is indicative rather than exhaustive, and the prescribed form and procedure for exercising the option are set by rules that change. Model your own numbers with a qualified chartered accountant before exercising an irrevocable option.
